report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is broadly right if it means *hypnosis has not been shown reliably to improve long-term smoking cessation*. It is more precise to say that evidence is **insufficient and uncertain**, rather than that hypnosis definitively does not help anyone.

The highest-quality synthesis is a 2019 Cochrane review of 14 trials. It found low- to very-low-certainty evidence, largely because trials were small, imprecise, and often at high risk of bias. The review found no reliable evidence that hypnotherapy produces better long-term quit rates than other behavioral support or quitting without assistance; if there is an effect, it is probably small.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6568235

Newer research has not resolved the problem. A 2024 randomized trial comparing hypnotherapy with cognitive-behavioral therapy notes that efficacy cannot yet be considered sufficiently proven because of major methodological limitations in the underlying literature.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10929270/

This does not mean hypnosis is necessarily harmful or useless as a personally motivating adjunct. But it should not replace treatments with substantially stronger evidence: behavioral counseling plus FDA-approved cessation medication (such as nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion, when appropriate). USPSTF recommends providing behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy to adults who use tobacco.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/tobacco-use-in-adults-and-pregnant-women-counseling-and-interventions
